claims.text: Conventional refractory high-entropy alloys containing tungsten, molybdenum, or tantalum are high-activation materials.
Conventional refractory HEAs exhibit excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
Tungsten-, molybdenum-, or tantalum-containing refractory HEAs tend to produce long-lived radioactive isotopes under neutron irradiation.
Vanadium, titanium, and chromium are low-activation refractory-element substitutes for tungsten, molybdenum, and tantalum.
Fusion plasma-facing components must operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K while exposed to intense irradiation, including neutrons.
Changing the elemental composition of a refractory HEA will modify its phase structure and microstructure.
The modified phase structure and microstructure will preserve mechanical integrity and irradiation resistance.
A nanocrystalline refractory HEA can exhibit high thermal stability and resistance to heavy-ion, dual-beam, and helium irradiation.
Substitution with vanadium, titanium, and chromium will lower the alloy's effective neutron activation cross-section.
Elements with lower neutron activation cross-sections produce fewer long-lived radionuclides upon neutron bombardment.
Maintaining a refractory high-entropy alloy framework supports high-temperature strength.
Maintaining a refractory high-entropy alloy framework supports microstructural stability against irradiation-induced damage.
Replacing tungsten, molybdenum, and tantalum with vanadium, titanium, and chromium will retain high-temperature strength comparable to tungsten-based HEAs.
The modified alloy will retain irradiation resistance comparable to tungsten-based HEAs.
The modified alloy will substantially reduce long-lived radionuclide production under fusion-relevant irradiation.
Tungsten is a leading plasma-facing material candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rate, and low tritium retention.
Tungsten-based refractory HEAs are currently under consideration as fusion plasma-facing materials.
Substitution may compromise phase stability or high-temperature mechanical performance.
Processing or additive-manufacturing scalability challenges may cause microstructural instability.
